title: What Assessment Actually Means
brief: Define assessment in plain terms using the module glossary definition: 'to determine or evaluate what students know or can do.' Introduce the two broad categories named in the module—traditional assessment and alternative assessment—and explain what distinguishes them: alternative assessment uses non-traditional methods such as self-assessment, peer assessment, portfolio assessment, student conferences, and performance-based assessment (role-plays, debates, presentations). Clarify that the choice between these categories is not arbitrary but depends on what was taught and what the teacher needs to find out. Reserve validity and reliability for their dedicated sections.

title: Formative and Summative Purposes: Choosing the Right Moment
brief: Draw on the module's distinction between formal and informal assessment and between formative and summative assessment as named in the glossary. Use the classroom example from the module: the teacher's rubric produces a final numeric score and grade (summative), while peer assessment forms are explicitly described as 'not a formal grade' and instead reflect students' experience of the discussion (formative). Explain that the same activity—a student-led discussion—can generate both kinds of evidence at once, and that teachers should decide in advance which purpose each task is serving before they select it. Keep the focus on task selection, not on how to design rubrics.

title: Matching the Task to What Was Taught
brief: Use the module's core principle that assessment should be aligned with learning goals: 'all of the learning goals for this activity are the same as the categories on the rubric' and 'the teacher aligns assessment with learning goals through the use of rubrics.' Explain that if a lesson used a communicative approach to develop speaking and listening, a pen-and-paper writing test would not match what was taught, whereas a performance-based task—such as leading or participating in a discussion—directly reflects the skills practiced. Introduce the module's definition of performance-based assessment (examining students' knowledge or skills as they complete tasks such as leading a discussion, participating in a debate, or creating a portfolio). Emphasise that task selection starts with the lesson objective: 'the statement of what the learners will be able to do once an activity or lesson is complete.'

title: Validity in Plain Terms: Does the Task Measure What You Claim?
brief: Explain validity without technical jargon, drawing directly on the module's language. The module states that alternative assessment 'helps test students' actual ability to use English for real-world communication, not just their knowledge of English.' Use this to frame validity as a practical question: does the task give evidence of the skill you said you were teaching? Connect this to the washback concept introduced in the module—the effect or influence that assessment has on learning and teaching. The module notes that if students 'don't think it is valid, don't see how it relates to their learning,' the washback effect can be negative; when students 'clearly see the connection to language learning outcomes,' the washback effect is likely positive. Present validity as something teachers can check by asking whether the task matches the stated objective.

title: Reliability in Plain Terms: Would the Score Hold Up?
brief: Define reliability as score consistency under comparable conditions and distinguish it sharply from validity. Show that a grammar quiz can measure the wrong skill consistently, while a speaking task can target the right skill but yield inconsistent scores. Give practical inter-rater safeguards for classroom performance assessment: analytic rubrics with observable descriptors, independent scoring of sample performances before grading, discussion of discrepancies, agreed scored examples, and double-scoring a small live sample. Emphasize that the strength of the consistency check should rise with the consequence of the score.

title: Practical Guidance for Selecting Assessment Tasks
brief: Synthesise the module's practical advice into a set of actionable selection criteria. Draw on the following source points: assessment tools should be 'clear, simple, and well aligned with learning goals'; students should see the assessment tool in advance so they know how they will be evaluated; tasks can be adapted for proficiency level (e.g., adjusting a rubric to a three-point scale for less advanced students, using less complex topics) and for class size (e.g., using more groups or smaller groups). Include the module's point that students become 'more familiar with and adept at using the forms/rubrics over time by practicing with them,' which means task selection also involves considering how familiar learners are with the assessment format. Frame all guidance as questions a teacher can ask before choosing a task.

title: Bloom's Taxonomy as a Task-Selection Tool
brief: Introduce the Bloom's Revised Taxonomy wheel described in the module, which organises learning into the cognitive levels Remember/Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create. Explain how the outer wheel's suggested products (e.g., survey, debate, role-play, self-evaluation, diagram, news article) and the middle wheel's level-related verbs (e.g., identify, compare, hypothesize, judge, invent) can help a teacher choose an assessment task that matches the cognitive demand of what was taught. If a lesson asked students to analyse, then a task asking them only to list or identify would not match the level of thinking practiced. Use this framework to reinforce the alignment principle from earlier sections: the cognitive level of the assessment task should correspond to the cognitive level of the learning activity.
